Photograph: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Russian sky full of our drones and not safe, Zelenskyy warns airlines Germany accuses Russia over Leipzig airport attack, citing solid evidence; Russian economy in risky ‘berserk mode’ says Putin development tsar. What we know on day 1,652 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Tue 1 Sep 2026 20.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned airlines and passengers against using Russian airspace because it will be filled with Ukrainian drones for the duration of the war. “Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” said Ukraine’s president. “Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such – not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account.” Vladimir Putin responded by calling Zelenskyy’s comments “a declaration of state terrorism”. Russia has started deliberately targeting the country’s railway network , Dan Sabbagh and Luke Harding write , with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv. Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and surrounds. At least 12 people died , with a dozen wounded, including three children. The railway has been a lifeline for Ukraine’s civilians in wartime, transporting millions and bringing world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham. The German government has concretely blamed Russia for the botched drone attack at Leipzig airport that unsuccessfully targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane , Kate Connolly writes from Berlin . Berlin said all indications were the Russian state provided the knowhow and equipment to “low-level agents” on the ground. Russia will face penalties – its consulate in Bonn will be closed, and Russian House, a purported cultural and science institute in Berlin, will be evicted after allegedly serving as a base for hybrid attacks and spying. A clampdown on Russia’s shadow fleet operations in German waters is planned. New blacklists of Russians would be drawn up and border controls tightened on Russians entering Germany, said the foreign minister, Johann Wadephul. The EU is preparing to toughen sanctions against Russia. Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase Read more The Russian wartime economy risks going “berserk”, Vladimir Putin’s ⁠international development envoy was quoted ⁠as saying on Tuesday. Boris Titov told business outlet RBC: “This is not an economy at all, it’s a kind of ‘berserk mode’ that can only exist for a ‌very limited time, and the necessity of which should be considered very carefully.” Titov’s ⁠comments echo a statement by Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, who argued that “killing a normal ​economy is equivalent to killing the whole ​country”. Andrei Klepach, the chief economist at the ​state development bank, lost his job last month after a public speech highlighting the economic challenges posed by the war. Ukraine ⁠damaged ⁠oil-processing units ​at ⁠Russia’s ⁠Novatek ​Ust-Luga ‌complex ‌in the Leningrad region during ‌an attack on Tuesday , ‌Kyiv’s ​military ⁠intelligence ​said. Key components of the oil refining facility and process equipment were damaged, said the GUR, and a major fire broke out. Russia attacked Ukraine’s Black Sea export infrastructure ⁠and a border crossing with Romania in the southern region of Odesa, Ukrainian officials said on Tuesday. Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz said Russia ​also damaged its Odesa combined heat ‌and power plant with missiles ‌and drones. Russia’s ⁠defence ⁠ministry said ⁠its forces ​struck ‌two ‌cargo ‌vessels in ‌the port ​of Pivdennyi, ⁠near ​Odesa, claiming they were carrying military goods. The claim could not be verified. David Petraeus has urged the UK to help lead a reinvention of Nato by adapting to a fundamental shift in warfare in the wake of the Ukraine war . The retired US army general and CIA ex-director told the House of Lords that Ukraine was the “defining military laboratory” of this century. Swift US technological advances in the defence sphere were not enough, Petraeus said, and nor was other nations simply purchasing better technology. He said Britain had shown “strategic clarity” after Russia’s full-scale invasion. “That now presents Britain with another opportunity: to become the first major western nation to organise its defence institutions around the new concept of warfare that Ukraine has been pioneering, and, in doing so, to help lead the transformation of Nato itself.” Russia’s presence at US-hosted G20 talks has caused unease among participants , the Canadian finance minister has said. Francois-Philippe Champagne said “it created discomfort, no doubt about that … The G7 has always been very united in our support for Ukraine and the Ukrainian people in the face of the illegal invasion and the suffering that we see.” Explore more on these topics Russia Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Europe Germany explainers Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.dw.com/en/middle-east-oil-ex.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NkgS Before the Iran war started, the Strait of Hormuz accounted for some 20% of the world’s daily crude oil and LNG supply [FILE: July 21, 2019] Image: Morteza Akhoundi/ISNA/Photoshot/picture alliance Advertisement Middle East crude oil exports , excluding Iran, rose back above pre-war levels in late September despite continued attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, according shipping data from trade intelligence firm Kpler . Exports exceeded the pre-war average of about 18 million barrels per day (bpd) on four days in the final week of September, reaching 19.5 million to 22.5 million bpd, according to the data and analytics platform. When the Strait of Hormuz closed following the start of the Iran war, the seven-day average non-Iranian crude leaving the region fell by 72% in 10 days, Kpler said. How was Hormuz bypassed? The recovery has relied on alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers. In September, about 40% of crude left the Gulf without crossing Hormuz, compared with only 17% before the Iran war . According to Kpler, more than 70% of the crude changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman in August. In comparison, almost no Gulf crude changed tankers in the Gulf of Oman before the war. Additionally, Saudi Arabia also increased exports through the Red Sea, while the UAE used its pipeline to Fujairah. The primary exporters of crude oil in the region were: Saudi Arabia the United Arab Emirates Iraq Iran, however, remains the major exception, with its exports still well below the pre-war average, primarily due to US policies. Attacks on ships around Hormuz continue Meanwhile, attacks on vessels have continued around Hormuz. At least seven incidents have been reported in recent weeks. On October 1, a tanker, Kazimah III, was reportedly struck by an unknown projectile, according to maritime intelligence firm Marisks. All crew members were evacuated safely. https://www.dw.com/en/can-we-regrow-dama.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O4G5 Regrowing underwater seagrass meadows takes time and patience Image: Geomar Advertisement Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag. They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive. The scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, says she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction. How seagrass is becoming a green building material To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared. "That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped." Why should we care about seagrass? Underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species . They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests. Around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet. On patrol with Mallorca's 'seagrass police' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," said Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance." But the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients. How can seagrass be replanted on a larger scale? Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier. Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach. "Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he said. The pressed strand of seagrass with biodegradable thread makes it easier to plant on longer stretches along the ocean floor Image: DW The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work. "We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig said. Could planting seeds be a solution? Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing new ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds. Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass. "Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said. "The big advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen. Together with replanted shoots, seeds can help regrow underwater meadows Image: DW Reusch from Geomar said they currently "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity." It takes time to see results Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later. Thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed. They then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the new crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one. "We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen said. "It's looking really good." This article is based on a Global Us video report.
